Recrystallization. A chemical purification technique used to dissolve an impure solid in a hot solvent and then cool the solution slowly. As the temperature drops, the desired compound precipitates out of the supersaturated solution as highly ordered, pure crystals, while the impurities remain dissolved in the surrounding solvent, known as the mother liquor.

The success of recrystallization depends on careful solvent selection based on temperature-dependent solubility. The ideal solvent has high solubility for the desired solute at elevated temperatures but poor solubility at low temperatures, while impurities remain soluble at all temperatures. Nucleation in supersaturated solutions can be induced by adding a tiny seed crystal or scratching the inner glass wall of the flask with a glass rod to create micro-particulate glass nucleation sites.

Removing colored impurities requires adding activated charcoal, also called decolorizing carbon, to the hot solution. The activated charcoal adsorbs high-molecular-weight organic impurities prior to hot gravity filtration, which removes insoluble impurities from the hot solution before crystallization of the target compound begins. After crystallization, vacuum filtration separates the crystal crop from the mother liquor, followed by a wash with ice-cold solvent.

For very small-scale work, a Craig tube is employed, a specialized glassware piece that combines dissolution, crystallization, and centrifugation-assisted filtration into a single device. Water is a common, non-toxic recrystallization solvent for polar organic compounds. The technique requires a two-step filtration process essential to achieving the purest product: hot gravity filtration to remove insoluble impurities and cold vacuum filtration to collect the final crystals.
